crux.for_the_english: Keep the story’s surface genuinely charming. Tatsuya must work in English as he works in a room—quick, amusing, at ease—and then, alone, reveal himself in the same untroubled voice: Mitsuyo is “beautiful prey,” her father is to be hooked, his debts and the mining concession are parts of one campaign. Do not signal villainy in advance, do not make the soliloquy brooding or conscience-stricken, and do not soften its sporting delight. The shock depends on how little his tone changes.
crux.point: This is a study in social plausibility: Tatsuya wins not despite being charming but because charm, rank, flattery and appetite are indistinguishable in the world he moves through. The horror is that his predation has no special register. It sounds like energy, competence, even good humour, until the reader hears what it is counting.
crux.why: He ingratiates himself with the inn maids, Zenpei, Mitsuyo’s whole household, and finally with officials, while privately treating a government coal-mine disposal as plunder and Mitsuyo as part of the payment. Zenpei is not simply deceived: his vanity and greed make him enjoy being deceived. Tsunao sees Tatsuya at once, but rectitude without social grace looks pale, pedantic and ungenerous beside him.

open_questions.question: How formal is the understanding between Mitsuyo and Tsunao? The text calls him a relative, has Zenpei speak of an existing promise and then announce the match broken, and gives the young people unmistakable intimacy, but it never cleanly labels him fiancé. Should English preserve that social legibility without naming it more definitely than the Japanese does?
open_questions.why_it_matters: If they are made merely cousins, Tatsuya’s demand loses force; if they are made explicitly engaged too early, the father-daughter teasing and Mitsuyo’s behaviour become narrower and less ambiguous.

open_questions.question: How far does Mitsuyo understand what she dislikes in Tatsuya? Her distaste is instinctive and bodily—he is ‘creepy,’ ‘strange’—rather than analytical. How much adult perception should the English allow into that intuition without making her either knowingly prophetic or merely petulant?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Her limited understanding is the point at which the comedy turns uneasy. Too much clarity makes her a judge of the plot; too little makes her father’s disposal of her seem weightless.

open_questions.question: At the close, is the narrator’s ignorance a genuine refusal of knowledge, a teasing invitation to infer, or both? Tatsuya has taken a wife; someone has thrown worldly trouble away for philosophy. The parallels invite identification of wife and philosopher without confirming either.
open_questions.why_it_matters: The last paragraph must not be resolved by tone. A knowing wink would say Tatsuya got Mitsuyo; a melancholy certainty would canonise Tsunao. The Japanese leaves marriage, ruin, renunciation and success suspended together.

open_questions.question: How much of Zenpei’s antiquarian display and of the mining intrigue is deliberate social satire, and how much is straight Meiji circumstantiality? The named vessels, screens, bribes, intermediaries, ordinance and first-filed application give corruption a material density that a brisk English summary would lose.
open_questions.why_it_matters: Cutting or clarifying these passages would make the plot cleaner but remove the world that makes it possible: status objects, cash, procedure and access are the real love-language between Zenpei and Tatsuya.

open_questions.question: The source twice gives Tsunao’s name with a different first character. Is that a printing or transcription accident to be silently normalised in a reading, or a point that needs editorial checking against the 1895 text?
open_questions.why_it_matters: No interpretive weight should be built on it until the witness is checked; the English should be consistent, but the edition should not invent a variant reading.

data.reading:
The crux is that this story’s surface genuinely charms. Okumura Tatsuya, a ministry secretary convalescing at a hot-spring inn, wins not despite being plausible but because plausibility is his instrument. He is quick with maids, landlords, an ageing rich man, officials and strangers; he knows what each person wishes to hear. Alone, in the same brisk and untroubled voice, he counts Mitsuyo as “beautiful prey,” her father as a man not to be let escape, and the disposal of the Kijima mine as a field for fees, bribes and leverage. Do not let English darken him in advance. He must first be good company. Nor should his private monologue become Gothic villainy: it is exuberant, comic, almost boyish in its appetite—“my trick,” “let’s begin,” speed is everything. The chill comes because nothing in his manner admits a conflict.

Almost everyone is taken in, and the text is precise about why. Zenpei, fat, laughing, Hotei-like, is not a passive fool. He loves the sound of Tatsuya’s rank, loves being recognised as a man of consequence, and wants the mine to repair earlier losses. Flattery gives his greed a respectable social form. When he agrees to pay and then, drunk on success, promises Tatsuya anything within his power, his earlier riddle has already shown where the bargain can go. English must let Zenpei be warm and ridiculous without making him harmless: the same doting father who submits to Mitsuyo’s pillow-fight can treat her, an hour later, as an asset whose transfer requires only timing.

Against Tatsuya stands Tojo Tsunao, a new philosophy graduate, and the translation stands or falls on refusing to rescue him into conventional heroism. Tsunao is right about Tatsuya immediately and almost completely. He is also pale, stiff, censorious and socially hopeless; he cannot make a necessary concession, cannot laugh off an insult, and can only leave. Seen through the inn’s eyes, and often through the narration’s, he looks like exactly what Tatsuya calls him: a pedant who will bury his life in empty theory. Yet his rigidity is the only form integrity takes here. If English gives him warm authority, the contest becomes melodrama. If it makes him merely absurd, Tatsuya has won the prose as he wins every room. He must hold his ground and make the reader pay for seeing that he is right.

Mitsuyo is the third term, and not a prize with a face. She first exists for Tatsuya as music behind a shoji, then as a glimpse, then, after the bath, as an almost embarrassingly lingering inventory of beauty. But once she speaks she becomes specific: spoiled, theatrical, quick, physically affectionate with her father, intoxicated by Tsunao’s arrival and childishly triumphant that her ally has come. Her repeated “truly, truly, truly” when she claims to be angry, her threats to break the incense box and spoil her father’s haori, her seizure of the air-pillow, are not decorative maidenliness. They establish a household in which indulgence is a language—and therefore a girl who can be bargained away in that same language. She is drawn to Tsunao naturally, without coy uncertainty; she also dislikes Tatsuya before she can say why, finding him uncanny rather than merely disagreeable. Keep both. Do not make her a knowing moral judge, and do not make her ignorant in a way that cancels her intuition.

The sound of the piece moves between three kinds of writing, and flattening that movement would be a major loss. The openings and transitions are lush Meiji scene-painting: long, tide-like sentences crowded with autumn bush-clover, lake water, waterfalls, inn corridors, thrushes and distant clappers. These passages should not be pruned into efficient setting. Their luxuriance is the world Tatsuya knows how to enjoy and exploit, and the lake-shore walk matters because beauty keeps offering an innocent explanation for his pursuit. Against this set the dialogue: Zenpei bluff and self-delighted, Mitsuyo bright with feminine Tokyo colloquialism and wheedling repetition, Tsunao formal to the point of bruising himself, Tatsuya shifting register for every listener. The third kind is procedure: ministry, bureau chief, supervisor, applications, a cabinet ordinance, first submission, commissions and annual “thanks-money.” It should remain concrete and slightly airless. Corruption here is not atmosphere. It is a sequence of doors, intermediaries and papers.

Certain repetitions carry structure. Tatsuya’s black beard is admired, joked about, accidentally insulted by Mitsuyo when she attacks Tsunao’s beard, and returns as a social sign of the fashionable man of the world. Zenpei’s laughter and Hotei bulk soften everything he does until they do not. Smoke from Tatsuya’s cigar punctuates moments of calculation, as if appetite itself were taking a pause to admire its plan. Mitsuyo’s “truly” in her tantrum is later answered, horribly, by the bargaining dialogue in which men say “certainly” and “without fail” over her. Preserve the echoes where they occur. Do not vary repeated phrases simply because English prose is taught to.

The most likely fluent failure is to tidy the intrigue into a clear contest between seducer and fiancé, with explanatory transitions and a decisive emotional climax. The Japanese instead lets domestic comedy take up room, lets a reception be described vessel by vessel, lets Tsunao walk out without farewells, and then accelerates. Zenpei returns from Tatsuya not even seeing his daughter’s tears because the mine has entered his head. That displacement—people looking straight past one another toward the desired object—is the story’s governing action. Look for it everywhere: Tatsuya at the lake still listening for a voice behind the shoji; Zenpei hearing rank rather than character; the family welcoming Tatsuya while Mitsuyo alone grows more hostile; mother and father counting Tsunao’s social failures when his moral perception has become inconvenient.

The ending must be left exactly as unresolved as the narrator leaves it. After Tatsuya asks for Mitsuyo as his “reward,” the text withdraws. It does not show acceptance, refusal, marriage, ruin or rescue. The narrator says he does not know what followed: Tatsuya is said to have taken a wife—who is she? Someone has cast off worldly trouble to devote a half-life to philosophy—who is he? Do not let word choice answer. The questions are inviting and desolate at once, and the final seasonal glance does not console. The most dangerous English additions would be a hint that virtue has been rewarded, that Tatsuya has been punished, or that Mitsuyo has understood her fate. None of that is given. What is given is a world so well arranged for Tatsuya that the reader must supply, and therefore fear, the likely result.
data.say: The reading is that this is a comedy of perfect social fit whose fluency is itself corrupt: beauty, manners, rank and bureaucratic procedure all conduct Tatsuya toward what he wants, while the people who resist him are either socially graceless or too young to know what their instinct has told them.

voice_takes.label: Polished surface, predatory undertow
voice_takes.line: Recommended first take. Narration should be supple and handsome enough to make the inn, the lake and Tatsuya himself pleasurable, with long scenic sentences allowed to gather before they break. Tatsuya speaks with easy masculine confidence and adapts instantly; alone he is quicker, blunter and more delighted, but never melodramatic. Zenpei is expansive, wheezing, pleased with himself. Mitsuyo is bright, spoiled, rapid and intimate, not quaint. Tsunao is clipped, elevated and awkward, his correctness costing him warmth. Wrong for this take: slangy modernisation, Victorian pastiche, or a narratorial sneer that tells the reader Tatsuya is false before his actions do.

voice_takes.label: Drier social satire
voice_takes.line: Narration plainer and more ironic, the scenic passages kept but tightened, the comedy of rank, antiques and fees allowed to sound almost dry. Tatsuya becomes a superior operator among operators; Zenpei funnier and more nakedly acquisitive; Tsunao’s stiffness more obviously a social defect. This gains speed and bite, but risks losing the genuine sensuous attraction of the hot-spring world and turning Mitsuyo’s danger into an epigram. Wrong for it: contemporary bureaucratic jargon or satire so broad that Zenpei ceases to be a doting father.

voice_takes.label: Fuller Meiji melodrama
voice_takes.line: Narration more formal and emotionally open, with the lake, music and first sight of Mitsuyo given romantic amplitude. Tatsuya is smoother and more dangerous, Tsunao more evidently the honourable lover, Mitsuyo more lyrical and imperilled. This is playable and may suit serial publication, but it is the riskiest take: it can settle ambiguities the story withholds and make Tatsuya’s late demand feel like a villain’s unmasking rather than the logical price of everything before it. Wrong for it: fainting innocence, Byronic darkness, or consolation at the close.
